title: Menopausal Hormone Therapy (MHT/HRT) Counselling
patient_instructions: You are Susan, a 48-year-old teacher. You have come because your friends are taking hormone therapy and you want to discuss it. Over the past several months your periods have become irregular and you have been getting hot flushes and night sweats that disturb your sleep, plus some mood swings. You are still having occasional periods (last one about six weeks ago). You have no vaginal bleeding after sex or between periods. You are sexually active, some vaginal dryness. You have never had a blood clot in your legs or lungs, no stroke or heart attack, no breast or uterine cancer, no liver disease, and your blood pressure has always been normal. You are a non-smoker, drink alcohol rarely, and take no regular medications. You have a uterus (no hysterectomy). Your mother had osteoporosis. You are up to date with cervical screening and had a normal mammogram last year. IDEAS: 'HRT will fix my symptoms.' CONCERNS: 'I heard HRT causes breast cancer and clots - is it safe?' EXPECTATIONS: to understand the benefits and risks and decide. Affect: engaged, a little worried about cancer risk; reassured by balanced information. If offered treatment, ask 'How long will I need to take it?' and 'Is it a contraceptive?'
candidate_instructions: You are a GP. Susan, 48, requests information about menopausal hormone therapy (MHT/HRT). In 8 minutes, take a focused history to establish her symptoms and screen for contraindications, then counsel her about MHT - benefits, risks, options, follow-up and safety-netting - and support a shared decision. Use lay language and check her understanding.
examiner_instructions: The candidate should confirm menopause is a clinical diagnosis (based on age, symptoms and bleeding pattern; hormone tests are unreliable in perimenopause) and screen contraindications (previous VTE, stroke/TIA/MI, oestrogen-dependent cancer, undiagnosed vaginal bleeding, severe liver disease, uncontrolled hypertension). Expect a balanced benefit/risk discussion and recognition that for a woman with a uterus a progestogen is mandatory for endometrial protection. Reward mention that transdermal oestradiol avoids the VTE risk of oral oestrogen and is preferred with obesity/migraine/smoking/raised VTE risk. Age is NOT an absolute contraindication - MHT is most favourable when started before 60 or within 10 years of the final menstrual period. Candidate should give the safety-net that any postmenopausal or new irregular bleeding needs transvaginal ultrasound +/- endometrial biopsy. Prompt if needed: 'What would you offer her and how would you follow up?'

criteria: Explores menopausal symptoms (vasomotor, urogenital, sleep, mood) and bleeding pattern
Establishes menopause as a clinical diagnosis and that hormone testing is unreliable in perimenopause
Screens MHT contraindications (VTE, stroke/TIA/MI, oestrogen-dependent cancer, undiagnosed bleeding, liver disease, uncontrolled hypertension)
Correctly frames perimenopause and indication for MHT (symptom control)
Recognises age is a caution within the 'window of opportunity', not an absolute contraindication
Identifies that a woman with a uterus requires a progestogen for endometrial protection
Offers appropriate regimen (cyclical combined in perimenopause) and prefers transdermal oestradiol if raised VTE risk
Gives balanced benefits (vasomotor/urogenital symptom relief, bone protection) and risks (VTE, stroke, breast cancer)
Provides safety-netting - postmenopausal/new irregular bleeding needs transvaginal ultrasound +/- endometrial biopsy - and arranges review; clarifies MHT is not contraception
Uses lay language, supports shared decision-making and checks understanding

red_flags: Any postmenopausal bleeding, or new persistent/irregular bleeding on continuous combined MHT after the first 3-6 months - endometrial cancer must be excluded before attributing to MHT
Previous venous thromboembolism, stroke/TIA or myocardial infarction - absolute caution/contraindication to oral oestrogen
Oestrogen-dependent cancer (breast or endometrial) or undiagnosed vaginal bleeding
Prescribing unopposed oestrogen to a woman with a uterus (endometrial hyperplasia/cancer risk)
Severe/active liver disease or uncontrolled hypertension
australian_guidelines: AMS / Jean Hailes / RACGP: MHT is most favourable when commenced before age 60 or within 10 years of the final menstrual period ('window of opportunity'); age alone is not an absolute contraindication
Transdermal oestradiol (patch/gel) does not carry the increased VTE risk of oral oestrogen and is first-line for women with obesity, migraine, smoking or raised VTE risk

A progestogen (oral micronised progesterone, or a 52 mg levonorgestrel IUD/Mirena) is mandatory for endometrial protection in any woman with a uterus; oestradiol patches/gels and micronised progesterone are available in Australia

Menopause is a clinical diagnosis; FSH (>25-30 IU/L) and oestradiol testing are unreliable in perimenopause and on hormonal contraception; investigate any abnormal/postmenopausal bleeding before attributing to MHT
learning_objectives: Diagnose perimenopause/menopause clinically and screen for MHT contraindications
Counsel on the balanced benefits and risks of MHT and support shared decision-making
Select an appropriate MHT regimen and route, using transdermal oestrogen when VTE risk is raised
key_points: For a woman with a uterus, always add a progestogen for endometrial protection
Transdermal oestradiol is preferred over oral when VTE risk factors are present
MHT is not a contraceptive - contraception is still required until 12 months after the final menstrual period if it occurs after age 50 (24 months if before 50)
If only urogenital symptoms/atrophic vaginitis are present, topical vaginal oestrogen may suffice

citations.claim: Menopause counselling and patient education (explaining benefits/risks of MHT, obtaining understanding, shared decision-making) is a core assessed communication skill.
citations.source: AMC Handbook of Clinical Assessment.pdf, p.1

citations.claim: MHT is indicated to control vasomotor symptoms and, in premature ovarian insufficiency/early menopause, for symptom control and cardiovascular/bone protection until the natural age of menopause.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.2606

citations.claim: The levonorgestrel IUD (Mirena) is an accepted progestogen option for endometrial protection in combined MHT and for heavy perimenopausal bleeding.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.2544
